# How to use this guide

Biostatistics and Research Methodology is half numericals and half theory. The numerical half (averages, SD, correlation, regression, t-tests, ANOVA, non-parametric tests, chi-square, factorial effects) rewards practice: you must be able to set out a table, apply the formula and state a conclusion in words. The theory half (sampling, hypothesis testing, research design, protocol, study types, clinical trial phases, software, optimization) rewards neat definitions, lists and tables. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, then rework every worked example on paper without looking, then attempt the question bank and the MCQs for that unit.

The notes follow the five units of the PCI syllabus. Unit 2 is the largest (regression, probability, sampling and the parametric tests) and is kept as one unit because the syllabus lists it that way; give it two days. Chi-square and the Wilcoxon signed rank test are not named in the syllabus list but are added to Unit 3 because they are standard non-parametric tests that appear in papers and practicals. A short note on logistic regression (named in the syllabus scope) is placed in Unit 4. No unit has been split or merged.

All data in the worked examples are example numbers made up for practice, not real product or patient data.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long (10-mark), short (5-mark) and very short (2-mark) questions. The very short ones are good warm-ups and help with MCQs.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer, with a worked numerical where one fits.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Introduction, averages, dispersion, correlation | Definition and uses of biostatistics, frequency distribution, mean/median/mode for grouped data, SD and CV, Karl Pearson's r, Spearman's rank correlation |
| 2 Regression, probability, sampling, parametric tests | Least-squares regression lines y on x and x on y, binomial and normal distribution with properties, types of sampling, Type I and II errors, SEM, the three t-tests, one-way ANOVA with LSD, two-way ANOVA |
| 3 Non-parametric tests, research, graphs, study design | Mann–Whitney and Wilcoxon, Kruskal–Wallis, Friedman, chi-square, need for research and DoE, plagiarism, graphs (histogram, pie, contour, response surface), sample size and power, protocol, cohort/observational/experimental studies, phases of clinical trials |
| 4 Blocking, regression modelling, software | Blocking and confounding in 2³ designs, hypothesis testing in simple and multiple regression, logistic regression idea, statistical problems in industry and clinical trials, Excel / SPSS / MINITAB / R steps |
| 5 Factorial design, RSM, optimization | Definition and advantages of factorial design, 2² and 2³ effects and interactions, central composite design, historical design, optimization techniques |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. In every numerical, write: data table → formula → substitution → answer with unit → conclusion in words. Most marks are for the method, so show each step even if your arithmetic slips.
2. For every test, state H0 and H1, the level of significance (5%), degrees of freedom, the table value and the decision ("calculated t 3.43 > table t 2.228, so H0 is rejected"). Carry the standard table values in your head: t(0.05) = 2.571 (df 5), 2.447 (df 6), 2.262 (df 9), 2.228 (df 10); χ²(0.05) = 3.84 (1 df), 5.99 (2 df), 7.81 (3 df); z = 1.96 and 2.58.
3. Keep the correction-factor layout for ANOVA (G, CF = G²/N, SST, SS between, SS error, df, MS, F) and always finish with an ANOVA table.
4. For choosing a test, draw the small "parametric vs non-parametric" match table (two independent groups, paired, three or more groups, association).
5. For theory questions, open with a one-line definition, then a numbered list or a table; for study types and trial phases a comparison table earns most marks.
6. Draw diagrams: normal curve with 68–95–99.7 areas, scatter diagrams, histogram, cube plot of a 2³ design, CCD layout, contour sketch, research-process flow chart.
7. Software questions want menu paths and steps, not screenshots: Excel → Data → Data Analysis; SPSS → Analyze; MINITAB → Stat → DOE; R → t.test(), lm(), aov().
8. Use a scientific calculator in statistics mode for Σx, Σx², Σxy, mean and SD, but still write the sums in the answer.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, practise one worked numerical each of: **grouped mean, median and mode with SD**, **Karl Pearson's r and the regression line**, **unpaired and paired t-tests**, **one-way ANOVA with LSD**, **Mann–Whitney U and chi-square**, and **effects of a 2² / 2³ factorial design**. Then read the theory tables for sampling, errors, study types, clinical trial phases, CCD and optimization.

**Numbers worth memorising**

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Normal areas | ±1σ 68.27%, ±1.96σ 95%, ±2σ 95.45%, ±2.58σ 99%, ±3σ 99.73% |
| z (two-tailed) | 1.96 at 5%, 2.58 at 1% |

| t (5%, two-tailed) | df 3: 3.182, 5: 2.571, 6: 2.447, 9: 2.262, 10: 2.228 |
| χ² (5%) | 1 df 3.84, 2 df 5.99, 3 df 7.81 |

| Large sample | n ≥ 30 |

| Bioequivalence | 90% CI of geometric mean ratio within 80–125% |

**Choosing a test**

| Data / question | Parametric | Non-parametric |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One sample vs a claimed value | One-sample t (z if n ≥ 30) | Wilcoxon signed rank |
| Two independent groups | Unpaired t | Mann–Whitney / Wilcoxon rank sum |
| Same subjects twice | Paired t | Wilcoxon signed rank |
| ≥ 3 independent groups | One-way ANOVA | Kruskal–Wallis |
| ≥ 3 treatments on same subjects | Two-way ANOVA | Friedman |
| Relation between two variables | Pearson r, regression | Spearman ρ |
| Counts in categories | — | Chi-square |

**Theory in one line each**

- Biostatistics: statistics applied to biology, medicine and pharmacy; descriptive vs inferential.
- Sampling: probability (simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster, multistage) vs non-probability (convenience, purposive, quota, snowball).
- H0 = no difference; Type I = rejecting a true H0 (α); Type II = accepting a false H0 (β); power = 1 − β.
- Fisher's principles of design: replication, randomisation, local control (blocking).
- Plagiarism: using others' words/ideas/data without credit; UGC 2018 regulations; cite and check similarity.
- Graphs: histogram (continuous classes), pie (parts of whole, angle = value/total × 360°), cube plot (2³ design), response surface (3D), contour plot (2D top view).
- Protocol: title, background, objectives, design, criteria, sample size, treatment, end points, safety, statistics, ethics, consent.
- Cohort: exposure → forward → relative risk. Case–control: disease → backward → odds ratio. RCT: randomised, controlled, blinded; strongest evidence.
- Trial phases: 0 microdose, I safety/PK in volunteers, II efficacy and dose in patients, III large confirmatory, IV post-marketing.
- Blocking removes nuisance variation; confounding hides the block effect in an unimportant interaction (ABC in a 2³ split into two blocks of four).
- Software: Excel (Analysis ToolPak), SPSS (Analyze menu), MINITAB (Stat → DOE, Quality Tools), R (t.test, lm, aov, chisq.test).
- Factorial design advantages: fewer runs, interactions measured, hidden replication, wider validity, model for optimization.
- CCD = factorial + axial + centre points; Box–Behnken has no corner points; historical design reuses past data.
- Optimization: Lagrangian, search, simplex, EVOP, canonical analysis, overlay contour, desirability function; confirm with check-point batches.

questions.answer:
1. Biostatistics: application of statistical methods (collection, organisation, analysis and interpretation of numerical data) to biological, medical and pharmaceutical problems.
2. Central tendency: a single value representing the centre of data. Qualities of a good average: rigidly defined, simple, based on all values, little affected by extremes, suitable for algebra.
3. Mean = Σx/n. Merits: uses every value, easy, suits further work. Demerits: pulled by extreme values, not for open classes or qualitative data.
4. Median = middle value of ordered data. Merits: not affected by extremes, suits skewed and ordinal data, can be found graphically (ogive). Demerits: ignores actual values, less suited to algebra.
5. Mode = most frequent value. Merits: easy, suits nominal data (most common brand). Demerits: may not exist or may be more than one; not based on all values.
6. Table: mid-points 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; fx = 3, 21, 60, 42, 18; Σfx = 144; N = 30; cf = 3, 10, 22, 28, 30.
7. Mean = Σfx/N = 144/30 = 4.8 min.
8. Median: N/2 = 15 → median class 4–6; L = 4, F = 10, f = 12, h = 2. Median = 4 + (15 − 10)/12 × 2 = 4.83 min.
9. Mode: modal class 4–6; f1 = 12, f0 = 7, f2 = 6. Mode = 4 + (12 − 7)/(24 − 7 − 6) × 2 = 4.91 min.
10. Check: 3 Median − 2 Mean = 14.5 − 9.6 = 4.9 min, close to the mode, so the distribution is nearly symmetrical.

questions.answer:
1. Correlation: degree and direction of linear relationship between two variables; it does not prove cause and effect.
2. Types: positive (both rise: concentration and absorbance), negative (one rises, other falls: drug content and storage time), zero; simple, multiple and partial; linear and non-linear.
3. Scatter diagram: plot (x, y) pairs; a narrow upward band = strong positive, downward band = negative, round cloud = none (draw three sketches).
4. Formula: r = Sxy/√(Sxx × Syy), where Sxy = Σxy − ΣxΣy/n, Sxx = Σx² − (Σx)²/n, Syy = Σy² − (Σy)²/n.
5. Sums: n = 5, Σx = 30, Σy = 1.54, Σxy = 11.28, Σx² = 220, Σy² = 0.5786.
6. Sxy = 11.28 − 9.24 = 2.04; Sxx = 220 − 180 = 40; Syy = 0.5786 − 0.47432 = 0.10428.
7. r = 2.04/√(40 × 0.10428) = 2.04/2.0424 = 0.9988.
8. Interpretation: almost perfect positive linear correlation; r² = 0.998, so 99.8% of the variation in absorbance is explained by concentration; the method obeys Beer's law in this range.
9. Properties of r: lies between −1 and +1; no unit; unaffected by change of origin and scale; geometric mean of the two regression coefficients.
10. Uses in pharmacy: linearity in analytical validation, IVIVC, dose–response, hardness vs disintegration.

questions.answer:
1. Dispersion: scatter of values around the average. Absolute measures (range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, SD) carry units; relative measures (coefficient of range, CV) are unit-free.
2. Range = largest − smallest; quick but uses only two values. Quartile deviation = (Q3 − Q1)/2. Mean deviation = Σ|x − x̄|/n. SD = √[Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)] for a sample; the best measure, used in further statistics.
3. Mean = 2505/10 = 250.5 mg.
4. Range = 255 − 247 = 8 mg; coefficient of range = 8/502 = 0.016.
5. Deviations: −2.5, 1.5, −0.5, −1.5, 0.5, −0.5, 2.5, −3.5, −0.5, 4.5; Σ|d| = 18 → mean deviation = 1.8 mg.
6. Squared deviations sum = 50.5; variance = 50.5/9 = 5.61; SD = 2.37 mg.
7. CV = 2.37/250.5 × 100 = 0.95%.
8. Interpretation: very low CV shows a uniform batch.
9. Properties of SD: not changed by adding a constant; multiplied by k when data are multiplied by k; ±1, ±2, ±3 SD cover about 68%, 95%, 99.7% of normal data.
10. Pharmaceutical uses: weight variation, content uniformity, precision (% RSD) of analytical methods.

1. Frequency distribution: arrangement of data in classes showing the number of observations (frequency) in each.
2. Steps: find the range; decide the number of classes (5–15; Sturges' rule k = 1 + 3.322 log10 N); class width = range/number of classes, rounded; write class limits (exclusive method, e.g. 0–2, 2–4); tally each value; count frequencies; add relative and cumulative frequency columns.
3. Terms: class limits, class mark = (lower + upper)/2, class width, relative frequency, cumulative frequency.

questions.answer:
1. SD measures the spread of individual observations around the mean: s = √[Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)].
2. SEM measures the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean: SEM = SD/√n; it is the SD of the distribution of sample means.
3. SD does not shrink with larger samples; SEM falls as n rises.
4. Use mean ± SD to describe data; mean ± SEM or a confidence interval to compare means.
5. SEM = 2.37/√10 = 2.37/3.162 = 0.75 mg.

questions.answer:
1. Skewness: lack of symmetry. Symmetrical: mean = median = mode. Positive skew: long right tail, mean > median > mode. Negative skew: long left tail, mean < median < mode.
2. Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness = (mean − mode)/SD.
3. Kurtosis: peakedness compared with a normal curve: leptokurtic (tall, sharp), mesokurtic (normal), platykurtic (flat).
4. Draw three curves for skewness and three for kurtosis.
5. Example: plasma half-life or survival time data are often positively skewed, so the median is reported.

questions.answer:
1. Regression: estimating the dependent variable from an independent variable using a fitted equation.
2. Least squares: choose a and b so that the sum of squared vertical deviations Σ(y − a − bx)² is minimum. Normal equations: Σy = na + bΣx; Σxy = aΣx + bΣx².
3. Solution: b = Sxy/Sxx; a = ȳ − bx̄. Line passes through (x̄, ȳ).
4. Sums: x̄ = 6, ȳ = 0.308; Sxy = 2.04, Sxx = 40, Syy = 0.10428.
5. y on x: b = 2.04/40 = 0.051; a = 0.308 − 0.306 = 0.002 → y = 0.002 + 0.051x.
6. x on y: b′ = 2.04/0.10428 = 19.56; a′ = 6 − 19.56 × 0.308 = −0.025 → x = −0.025 + 19.56y.
7. Check: 0.051 × 19.56 = 0.998 = r²; r = 0.999.

1. t-test (Student's t, W.S. Gosset): test of significance for means of small samples (n < 30) when population SD is unknown.
2. Assumptions: random independent samples, normal population, quantitative data, equal variances for the unpaired test.
3. Types: one-sample (sample mean vs a value), unpaired/pooled (two independent groups), paired (same subjects twice).
4. H0: µA = µB; H1: µA ≠ µB; α = 0.05, two-tailed.
5. A: mean 84.0, Σ(x − x̄)² = 50; B: mean 78.0, Σ(x − x̄)² = 42.
6. Pooled variance sp² = (50 + 42)/(6 + 6 − 2) = 9.2; sp = 3.03.
7. SE of difference = √[9.2(1/6 + 1/6)] = 1.751.
8. t = (84 − 78)/1.751 = 3.43; df = 10; table t(0.05, 10) = 2.228.
9. Decision: 3.43 > 2.228, reject H0; formulation A dissolves significantly more (P ≈ 0.006).
10. Check of equal variances: F = 10.0/8.4 = 1.19 < F(5,5) 5.05, so pooling was valid.

1. ANOVA (R.A. Fisher): compares three or more means in one test by splitting total variation into between-group and within-group (error) parts; avoids inflated Type I error of many t-tests.
2. Assumptions: normal populations, equal variances, independent random samples, additive effects.
3. Totals: 20.8, 24.8, 22.8; means 5.2, 6.2, 5.7; G = 68.4; N = 12; CF = 68.4²/12 = 389.88; Σx² = 392.22.

6. ANOVA table: Between 2.00, df 2, MS 1.00; Within 0.34, df 9, MS 0.0378; F = 26.5.
7. Table F(2, 9) at 5% = 4.26; F > table → binders differ significantly.
8. LSD = t(0.05, 9) × √(2 × MSE/n) = 2.262 × √(2 × 0.0378/4) = 0.31 kg.
9. Differences: starch − PVP 1.0, starch − MCC 0.5, MCC − PVP 0.5; all > 0.31 → all pairs differ; starch gives the hardest tablets.

1. Normal distribution: continuous, bell-shaped probability distribution defined by mean µ and SD σ; f(x) = [1/(σ√2π)] e^[−(x − µ)²/2σ²].
2. Properties: symmetrical about the mean; mean = median = mode; tails asymptotic to the x-axis; total area 1; inflexion points at µ ± σ; skewness zero, mesokurtic.
3. Areas: µ ± 1σ 68.27%, µ ± 1.96σ 95%, µ ± 2σ 95.45%, µ ± 2.58σ 99%, µ ± 3σ 99.73% (draw the bell curve with these marked).
4. Standard normal variate z = (x − µ)/σ, mean 0, SD 1; areas read from z tables.
5. (a) z for 240 = −2, for 260 = +2; area = 0.9545 → 95.45% of tablets.
6. (b) z = (258 − 250)/5 = 1.6; area beyond 1.6 = 0.0548 → about 5.5% of tablets.
7. Importance: basis of z, t and F tests, confidence intervals and control charts; central limit theorem makes means of large samples nearly normal.
8. Examples: tablet weight, assay values, measurement errors, body height.

questions.answer:
1. Type I error (α): rejecting H0 when it is true (false positive), e.g. saying an ineffective drug works or rejecting a good batch (producer's risk in QC).
2. Type II error (β): accepting H0 when it is false (false negative), e.g. missing a useful drug or accepting a bad batch (consumer's risk).
3. Table: Reject H0 & H0 true = Type I; Accept H0 & H0 false = Type II; other two cells are correct decisions.
4. Power = 1 − β: probability of detecting a real difference; usually 80–90%.
5. Power increases with larger sample size, larger true difference, less variability and larger α. Lowering α alone raises β.

Probability sampling (known chance of selection): simple random (lottery, random numbers: 20 tablets from a batch); systematic (every kth unit after a random start: every 100th tablet off the press); stratified (divide into strata, sample each: beginning, middle, end of batch); cluster (choose whole groups at random: hospitals or villages); multistage (random selection in stages).
2. Non-probability sampling: convenience (easily available patients), purposive/judgement (experts), quota (fixed numbers per category), snowball (subjects refer others).
3. Probability methods allow valid statistical inference; non-probability methods risk bias.
4. Sampling error falls with larger sample size; non-sampling errors arise from bias and measurement mistakes.

questions.answer:
1. Null hypothesis (H0): no difference or no effect (µ1 = µ2).
2. Alternative hypothesis (H1): there is a difference (two-tailed) or a difference in one stated direction (one-tailed).
3. Level of significance (α): accepted risk of rejecting a true H0, usually 5% or 1%; P value = probability of a result this extreme if H0 is true.
4. Degrees of freedom: number of values free to vary, e.g. n − 1 for one sample.
5. Steps: state H0/H1 → choose α and tails → choose test and compute statistic → find table value for df → compare and decide → state conclusion.

questions.answer:
1. Two-way ANOVA studies two sources of variation (factor A rows, factor B columns) together, e.g. formulations and analysts.
2. Partition (without replication): SST = SS rows + SS columns + SS error; df r − 1, c − 1, (r − 1)(c − 1); F for rows = MSR/MSE, for columns = MSC/MSE.
3. SS rows = Σ(row total²)/c − CF; SS columns = Σ(column total²)/r − CF.
4. With replication it also tests the interaction A × B.
5. Difference: one-way has one factor and error only; two-way removes a second source (block) from error, so tests are more sensitive (randomised block design).
6. Example (example numbers): three formulations × four analysts gave F(formulation) = 33.3 and F(analyst) = 10.2, both above table values 5.14 and 4.76.

questions.answer:
1. Non-parametric (distribution-free) tests: do not assume a normal population; work on ranks or counts; used for ordinal data, skewed data, very small samples.
2. Comparison: parametric needs normality and equal variances, uses mean/SD, more powerful when valid (t, ANOVA); non-parametric needs no distribution, uses median/ranks, slightly less powerful (Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal–Wallis, Friedman, chi-square).
3. Mann–Whitney U: compares two independent groups (non-parametric form of unpaired t-test).
4. Steps: H0 equal distributions → rank all values together → rank sums R1, R2 → U1 = n1n2 + n1(n1 + 1)/2 − R1; U2 = n1n2 − U1 → smaller U vs table.
5. Ranks: A 2, 4, 1, 6, 3 (R = 16); B 9, 7, 8, 5, 10 (R = 39).
6. U(A) = 25 + 15 − 16 = 24; U(B) = 25 − 24 = 1.
7. Table critical U (n1 = n2 = 5, 5% two-tailed) = 2; U = 1 ≤ 2 → reject H0.
8. Conclusion: drug A gives significantly faster relief.
9. Wilcoxon rank sum gives the same decision (W = 16 ≤ 17).
10. For n > 20, use z = (U − n1n2/2)/√[n1n2(n1 + n2 + 1)/12].

questions.answer:
1. Classification: Observational (descriptive: case report, case series, cross-sectional; analytical: case–control, cohort) and Experimental (randomised controlled trial, non-randomised trial, field/community trial).
2. Observational studies: investigator only observes, does not give exposure; used when experiments are unethical or impractical.
3. Cross-sectional: exposure and outcome at one time; prevalence. Case–control: start with cases and controls, look back for exposure; odds ratio; quick, good for rare diseases; recall bias.
4. Cohort: disease-free group classified by exposure and followed forward; gives incidence and relative risk; can study many outcomes; costly, long, drop-outs; prospective or retrospective.
5. Experimental studies: investigator assigns treatment, randomisation, control (placebo or standard), blinding; RCT gives strongest evidence of cause and effect.
6. Phase 0: microdose in a few subjects, early pharmacokinetics.
7. Phase I: about 20–80 healthy volunteers (patients for toxic drugs); safety, tolerability, maximum tolerated dose, pharmacokinetics.
8. Phase II: about 100–300 patients; efficacy, dose range, short-term safety.
9. Phase III: about 1,000–3,000 or more patients, multicentre, against placebo or standard; confirms efficacy and safety; basis of marketing approval.
10. Phase IV: post-marketing surveillance; rare and long-term adverse effects, new uses, pharmacovigilance. All phases need ethics approval, informed consent and GCP.

questions.answer:
1. Chi-square test: compares observed (O) and expected (E) frequencies: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E.
2. Applications: goodness of fit, test of independence (association) in contingency tables, homogeneity of proportions.
3. Conditions: counts not percentages, independent observations, random sample, expected frequency ≥ 5 per cell; Yates' correction for small 2 × 2; Fisher's exact test for very small tables.
4. df = (r − 1)(c − 1).
5. Table: drug 30 cured / 10 not; placebo 18 / 22; totals 48 / 32; N = 80.
6. E = row total × column total/N: cured 24, not cured 16 in each row.
7. χ² = 36/24 + 36/16 + 36/24 + 36/16 = 1.5 + 2.25 + 1.5 + 2.25 = 7.5.
8. df = 1; table χ² = 3.84; 7.5 > 3.84 → reject H0; cure is associated with the drug (P ≈ 0.006).
9. Shortcut: χ² = N(ad − bc)²/[(a + b)(c + d)(a + c)(b + d)] = 7.5. With Yates' correction χ² = 6.30, still significant.
10. Limitation: shows association, not strength or cause.

questions.answer:
1. Kruskal–Wallis H test: non-parametric equivalent of one-way ANOVA for three or more independent groups.
2. H = [12/N(N + 1)] ΣR²/n − 3(N + 1); compare with χ² at k − 1 df.
3. Ranks of all 12 values: X 2, 6, 1, 4 (R = 13); Y 10, 12, 8, 11 (R = 41); Z 5, 7, 3, 9 (R = 24).
4. H = (12/156)(169/4 + 1681/4 + 576/4) − 39 = 0.0769 × 606.5 − 39 = 7.65.
5. χ²(2 df, 5%) = 5.99; H > 5.99 → treatments differ significantly.

questions.answer:
1. Friedman test: non-parametric equivalent of two-way ANOVA (randomised block) for k ≥ 3 related treatments given to the same b subjects.
2. Steps: rank treatments within each subject; add ranks Rj per treatment; χr² = [12/bk(k + 1)]ΣRj² − 3b(k + 1); compare with χ² at k − 1 df.
3. Example (example numbers): 5 panellists scored 3 flavours; rank sums 6, 15, 9.
4. χr² = [12/(5 × 3 × 4)](36 + 225 + 81) − 60 = 0.2 × 342 − 60 = 8.4.
5. 8.4 > 5.99 (2 df) → flavour preference differs; the flavour with rank sum 15 is preferred.

1. Sample size determination: finding the number of subjects needed to detect a stated difference with given α and power, without wasting resources.
2. Factors: level of significance (α), power (1 − β), smallest important difference, variability (SD), design (paired/parallel), number of groups, expected drop-outs.
3. Formula (two means): n per group = 2(zα/2 + zβ)²σ²/d².
4. n = 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)² × 100/25 = 2 × 7.84 × 4 = 62.7 → 63 per group.
5. With 90% power (zβ = 1.28) about 84 per group; add about 10% for drop-outs.

2. Need in pharmacy: new drugs and dosage forms, improving products, proving safety and efficacy, solving manufacturing problems, rational drug use, evidence-based practice.
3. Need for DoE: one-factor-at-a-time needs many runs and misses interactions; DoE changes several factors together, estimates main effects and interactions with few runs, estimates error, gives a model for prediction and optimization, supports QbD and design space.

questions.answer:
1. Histogram: adjacent bars over continuous class intervals; area ∝ frequency; shows the shape of a distribution (tablet weights).
2. Pie chart: circle divided into sectors; angle = value/total × 360°; shows parts of a whole (share of dosage forms).
3. Cubic graph (cube plot): 3D cube with the response at each corner of a 2³ factorial design; shows effects of three factors at once.
4. Response surface plot: 3D surface of predicted response against two factors from a fitted model; peaks/valleys show optimum.
5. Contour plot: 2D top view of the response surface; lines join equal responses; overlay plots show the design space.
6. All graphs need a title, labelled axes with units and a legend.

questions.answer:
1. Blocking: grouping runs into uniform sets (day, batch of raw material, operator) so that nuisance variation is removed from experimental error; randomise within blocks; replicates can be blocks.
2. Confounding: when a single replicate must be split into blocks smaller than 2^k, an effect is deliberately made inseparable from the block difference; a high-order interaction (believed negligible) is chosen.
3. 2³ runs: (1), a, b, ab, c, ac, bc, abc.
4. Signs of ABC (product of A, B, C signs): (1) −, a +, b +, ab −, c +, ac −, bc −, abc +.
5. Block 1 (ABC −): (1), ab, ac, bc (principal block, contains (1)); Block 2 (ABC +): a, b, c, abc.
6. Defining contrast method: L = x1 + x2 + x3 (mod 2); L = 0 → block 1, L = 1 → block 2.
7. Effect: block difference = ABC contrast; e.g. with responses 62, 74, 55, 69, 50, 81, 47, 79 (example numbers), block totals 259 and 258 and ABC contrast −1 are the same quantity.
8. Main effects and two-factor interactions are unaffected (each has two + and two − in every block).
9. Four blocks: confound two effects (AB, AC) and their generalised interaction (BC) also; blocks (1)/abc, a/bc, b/ac, ab/c.
10. Complete vs partial confounding: same effect in every replicate vs different effects in different replicates.

questions.answer:
1. Purpose: check that the fitted relation is real and each coefficient is non-zero.

6. Example (hardness model, example numbers): y = 0.767 + 0.48x1 + 0.75x2; F = 4.005/0.0544 = 73.6 > F(2, 3) 9.55; t(b1) = 10.3, t(b2) = 6.4 > 3.18; R² 0.98, adjusted 0.967.

questions.answer:
1. Confounding: deliberate design in which an effect (usually a high-order interaction) cannot be separated from block differences, used when a replicate must be split into smaller blocks.
2. The confounded effect is sacrificed; other effects are estimated clearly.
3. Complete confounding: the same effect is confounded in all replicates, so no information on it remains.
4. Partial confounding: different effects are confounded in different replicates; each effect is estimated from replicates where it is not confounded.
5. Example: 2³ in two blocks confounding ABC: block 1 (1), ab, ac, bc; block 2 a, b, c, abc.

questions.answer:
1. Blocking groups experimental units or runs into homogeneous blocks (same day, same raw-material lot, same machine or analyst).
2. Variation between blocks (nuisance factor) is removed from the error term.
3. This gives a smaller error and more sensitive tests of the factors of interest.
4. Treatments are randomised within each block.
5. Examples: randomised block design, running each replicate of a factorial on a different day, crossover trials with subjects as blocks.
6. If blocks are smaller than a full replicate, confounding is needed.

3. Chi-square steps: define the two categorical variables with value labels → enter data (or weight cases by count) → Analyze → Descriptive Statistics → Crosstabs → put one variable in Rows and one in Columns → Statistics → tick Chi-square → Cells → tick Observed and Expected → OK.
4. Read Pearson chi-square value, df and Asymptotic Significance; use Continuity Correction or Fisher's exact test for small 2 × 2 tables.
questions.question: Give the features of SPSS and the steps to perform a chi-square test in it.

questions.answer: In a confounded factorial, the principal block is the block that contains the run (1) (all factors at the low level); other blocks are obtained from it by multiplying with a run not in it.
questions.question: What is meant by the principal block?

questions.answer: R² always rises when a variable is added, even a useless one; adjusted R² penalises extra variables, so it is better for comparing models.
questions.question: Why is adjusted R² preferred over R² in multiple regression?

questions.answer:
1. Factorial design: every level of each factor combined with every level of the others; k factors at 2 levels need 2^k runs.
2. Terms: factor, level (coded −1, +1), response, run, main effect, interaction.
3. 2² design: four runs (1), a, b, ab; draw the square with A on the x-axis and B on the y-axis.
4. Effect A = ½[(a + ab) − ((1) + b)] = ½[(6 + 13) − (4 + 7)] = 4.0 min.
5. Effect B = ½[(b + ab) − ((1) + a)] = ½[(7 + 13) − (4 + 6)] = 5.0 min.
6. Interaction AB = ½[((1) + ab) − (a + b)] = ½[(4 + 13) − (6 + 7)] = 2.0 min.
7. Model: y = 7.5 + 2.0xA + 2.5xB + 1.0xAxB.
8. Interpretation: A raises DT by 2 min at low B but 6 min at high B; non-parallel interaction plot.
9. Advantages: several factors in fewer runs; detects interactions; hidden replication (all runs used for every effect); results valid over a range; gives a model for optimization; orthogonal, easy analysis.
10. Limitations: runs rise fast with k; two levels cannot show curvature (add centre points or use RSM).
questions.question: Define factorial design. Explain the 2² factorial design and calculate the main effects and interaction for the disintegration time (min) data (example numbers): (1) = 4, a = 6, b = 7, ab = 13. List the advantages of factorial design.

questions.answer:
1. 2³ design: three factors A, B, C at two levels → eight runs; estimates A, B, C, AB, AC, BC, ABC.
2. Table of signs in standard order (1), a, b, ab, c, ac, bc, abc; interaction columns = products of main columns; each column has four + and four −.
3. Contrast = Σ(sign × response); effect = contrast/4; SS = contrast²/8.
4. Contrasts: A 89, B −17, C −3, AB 3, AC 37, BC 7, ABC −1 (total 517, mean 64.6).
5. Effects: A 22.25, B −4.25, C −0.75, AB 0.75, AC 9.25, BC 1.75, ABC −0.25.
6. SS: A 990.1, B 36.1, C 1.1, AB 1.1, AC 171.1, BC 6.1, ABC 0.1; total 1205.9.
7. Pool AB, BC, ABC as error: SS 7.375, df 3, MS 2.458.
8. F: A 402.8, B 14.7, C 0.46, AC 69.6; table F(1, 3) = 10.13 → A, B and AC significant, C not.
9. Yates' algorithm gives the same contrasts (column 3: 517, 89, −17, 3, −3, 37, 7, −1).
10. Model y = 64.6 + 11.1xA − 2.1xB + 4.6xAxC; show cube plot and Pareto chart of effects.
questions.question: Explain the 2³ factorial design with a table of signs. Calculate the effects for the % drug released (example numbers): (1) 62, a 74, b 55, ab 69, c 50, ac 81, bc 47, abc 79, and identify significant effects.

questions.answer:
1. RSM: statistical and mathematical techniques to model a response affected by several factors and find the optimum; uses a second-order model y = b0 + Σbixi + Σbijxixj + Σbiixi².
2. Sequence: screening → first-order design and steepest ascent → second-order design → model checks (ANOVA, lack of fit, R²) → contour and 3D plots → optimization → check-point batches.
3. CCD: 2^k factorial points + 2k axial points at ±α + n0 centre points; N = 2^k + 2k + n0 (k = 2: 13 runs with 5 centre points).
4. α: rotatable (2^k)^¼ = 1.414 for k = 2, 1.682 for k = 3; face-centred α = 1; inscribed design keeps axial points at ±1; five levels per factor in rotatable CCD. Draw the CCD star diagram.
5. Advantages: efficient quadratic model, sequential build from a factorial, estimates curvature and pure error. Box–Behnken is an alternative with no corner points.
6. Optimization: finding factor levels giving the best response within constraints.
7. Methods: classical calculus and Lagrangian (constraints by Lagrange multipliers); search (grid) method; simplex (moving triangle away from worst response); evolutionary operation (small changes during production); canonical analysis; overlay contour plots (design space); desirability function (overall D = geometric mean of individual d).
8. Historical design: model built from existing past data; cheap but non-orthogonal, must be confirmed.
9. Applications: tablets, SR matrices, microspheres, nanoparticles, emulsions, analytical methods, QbD design space.
10. Always confirm the optimum with check-point batches and low prediction error.
questions.question: What is response surface methodology? Explain the central composite design and the optimization techniques used in pharmaceutical formulation.

questions.answer:
1. Advantages: fewer runs for the same information; measures interactions, which OFAT cannot; every run contributes to every effect (hidden replication, high precision); conclusions valid over a range of conditions; gives a predictive model; orthogonal effects; simple analysis by sign table or software.
2. Limitations: number of runs grows as 2^k; two-level designs detect only linear effects (curvature needs centre points or RSM); high-order interactions hard to interpret; fractional designs needed for many factors, with aliasing.
questions.question: List the advantages and limitations of factorial design over one-factor-at-a-time experiments.

questions.answer:
1. CCD: the most common second-order response surface design.
2. Parts: 2^k factorial (cube) points at ±1, 2k axial (star) points at ±α, n0 centre points.
3. Runs: N = 2^k + 2k + n0 (k = 3: 8 + 6 + 6 = 20).
4. α = (2^k)^¼ for rotatability (1.414, 1.682); α = 1 for face-centred design.
5. Fits a full quadratic model; centre points give pure error and test curvature; can be built on a completed factorial.
6. Draw the 2-factor CCD: square with four corners, four star points on the axes and centre point.
questions.question: Write a note on central composite design.

questions.answer:
1. Many formulations must satisfy several responses at once (dissolution, hardness, friability).
2. Desirability function: each response is converted to an individual desirability d between 0 (unacceptable) and 1 (ideal); overall desirability D = geometric mean of all d values; software searches for factor settings with the highest D.
3. Overlay contour plots: contour plots of each response drawn for the two factors and superimposed; the region where every response meets its limits is the feasible region or design space.
4. Both are used in DoE software and in Quality by Design; the chosen point is confirmed by check-point batches.
questions.question: Explain the use of the desirability function and overlay contour plots in optimization.

questions.answer:
1. Simplex method: a geometric figure with k + 1 vertices (triangle for two factors) is set up; experiments are run at the vertices; the worst vertex is reflected through the centre of the others to a new point; the figure moves step by step towards the optimum; needs no model; used for analytical and formulation optimization.
2. Evolutionary operation (EVOP): small, planned changes in process variables are made around the normal operating point during routine production; responses are compared after several cycles; the operating point is moved in the better direction; improves the process without separate experiments or loss of product.
questions.question: Explain the simplex method and evolutionary operation as optimization techniques.

questions.answer:
1. Historical data design: a response surface model built from data already available (earlier development batches, production records, past experiments) instead of new planned runs.
2. Merits: no new experiments, saves time and cost, uses valuable existing knowledge, useful for troubleshooting and retrospective process understanding.
3. Limitations: data not planned, so factors may be correlated and ranges narrow; some combinations missing; uncontrolled variables can bias the model; the model must be checked and confirmed with new runs.

# Unit 1: Introduction, central tendency, dispersion and correlation

Every pharmacy decision rests on numbers that vary: tablet weights, assay results, blood pressure readings, cure rates. Statistics gives the tools to describe that variation, compare groups fairly and decide whether a difference is real or just chance. This unit builds the base: what statistics is, how data are arranged in a frequency distribution, how to find the "centre" of data (mean, median, mode), how spread out the data are (range, standard deviation) and how two variables move together (correlation).

All numbers in the worked examples below are **example numbers** made up for practice, not real product data.

## 1.1 Statistics and biostatistics

**Statistics** is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting numerical data so that sound conclusions can be drawn in the face of variation and uncertainty.

**Biostatistics** is statistics applied to biological, medical and pharmaceutical problems: clinical trials, bioequivalence, quality control of medicines, epidemiology and laboratory experiments.

**Two branches**

| Branch | What it does | Pharmacy example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Descriptive statistics | Summarises data by tables, graphs, averages and spread | Mean weight and SD of 20 tablets |
| Inferential statistics | Draws conclusions about a population from a sample, with a stated risk of error | Is the new formulation's dissolution better than the old one? |

**Uses of biostatistics in pharmacy**

1. Quality control: weight variation, content uniformity, control charts, acceptance sampling of batches.
2. Formulation development: design of experiments and optimization of a formula.
3. Clinical trials: sample size, randomisation, comparing treatments, safety analysis.
4. Bioavailability and bioequivalence: comparing AUC and Cmax of test and reference products.
5. Pharmacology: dose–response curves, ED50 and LD50 estimation in animal studies.
6. Stability studies: regression of drug content against time to set the shelf life.
7. Analytical method validation: linearity (regression), precision (SD, RSD), accuracy.
8. Epidemiology and pharmacovigilance: rates of disease and adverse reactions.

**Limitations of statistics**

- It studies groups, not single individuals.
- Results are true only on average and only within stated chances of error.
- It can be misused: biased samples or wrong tests give misleading answers.
- It deals with data that can be expressed in numbers (or counted).

## 1.2 Basic terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Population | The whole group about which we want to conclude (all tablets of a batch) |
| Sample | A part of the population actually studied (20 tablets drawn from the batch) |
| Parameter | A value describing a population (population mean µ, SD σ) |
| Statistic | A value calculated from a sample (sample mean x̄, SD s) |
| Variable | A characteristic that changes from one unit to another |
| Observation | One recorded value of a variable |

**Types of data (variables)**

```text
Data
 ├── Qualitative (categorical)
 │     ├── Nominal  : names only, no order       (blood group, gender, brand)
 │     └── Ordinal  : ordered categories         (pain: mild / moderate / severe)
 └── Quantitative (numerical)
       ├── Discrete   : counts, whole numbers     (number of defective tablets)
       └── Continuous : any value in a range      (weight, temperature, plasma level)
```

Measurement scales: nominal, ordinal, interval (equal steps, no true zero, e.g. °C) and ratio (true zero, e.g. weight, concentration).

**Sources of data:** primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator (a trial, a survey); secondary data are taken from existing records (hospital records, published reports).

## 1.3 Frequency distribution

Raw data are hard to read. A **frequency distribution** groups the observations into classes and shows how many fall in each.

**Steps to form a grouped frequency distribution**

1. Find the range (largest − smallest value).
2. Decide the number of classes, usually 5 to 15. Sturges' rule gives a guide: k = 1 + 3.322 log10 N.
3. Class width h = range ÷ number of classes, rounded to a convenient value.
4. Write class limits so that every value fits in exactly one class (exclusive method: 0–2, 2–4, where the upper limit is not included).
5. Tally each observation and count the frequency.

**Useful terms**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Class limits | Lowest and highest values of a class |
| Class mark (mid-point) | (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2 |
| Class width | Upper limit − lower limit |
| Relative frequency | Class frequency ÷ total frequency |
| Cumulative frequency (cf) | Frequency of a class plus all classes before it |

**Worked frame (example numbers): disintegration time of 30 tablets**

| Time (min) | Frequency f | Mid-point x | f × x | cf |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–2 | 3 | 1 | 3 | 3 |
| 2–4 | 7 | 3 | 21 | 10 |
| 4–6 | 12 | 5 | 60 | 22 |
| 6–8 | 6 | 7 | 42 | 28 |
| 8–10 | 2 | 9 | 18 | 30 |
| Total | N = 30 | | Σfx = 144 | |

This same table is used for the grouped mean, median and mode below.

## 1.4 Measures of central tendency

A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents the centre of a set of data. A good average is rigidly defined, easy to understand, based on all observations, not much affected by extreme values and suitable for further mathematical work.

### 1.4.1 Arithmetic mean

**Ungrouped data:** x̄ = Σx ÷ n

**Grouped data (direct method):** x̄ = Σfx ÷ N

**Assumed mean (short-cut) method:** x̄ = A + (Σfd ÷ N), where d = x − A; with step deviation, x̄ = A + (Σfd′ ÷ N) × h, where d′ = (x − A) ÷ h.

Properties: the sum of deviations from the mean is zero; the sum of squared deviations is least when taken from the mean; it uses every value but is pulled by extreme values.

**Worked example 1 (ungrouped, example numbers).** Weights (mg) of 10 tablets: 248, 252, 250, 249, 251, 250, 253, 247, 250, 255.

- Σx = 2505, so mean = 2505 ÷ 10 = **250.5 mg**.
- Arranged: 247, 248, 249, 250, 250, 250, 251, 252, 253, 255. With n even, median = average of 5th and 6th values = (250 + 250) ÷ 2 = **250 mg**.
- Mode = most frequent value = **250 mg** (occurs three times).

**Worked example 2 (grouped, from the table in 1.3).** Mean = Σfx ÷ N = 144 ÷ 30 = **4.8 min**.

### 1.4.2 Median

The median is the middle value when data are arranged in order; half the values lie below it and half above.

- Ungrouped: arrange in order; if n is odd, median = value at position (n + 1)/2; if n is even, average of the two middle values.
- Grouped: Median = L + [(N/2 − F) ÷ f] × h

where L = lower limit of the median class, N/2 locates the median class from the cf column, F = cf of the class before the median class, f = frequency of the median class, h = class width.

**Worked example (grouped).** N/2 = 15. The cf column first passes 15 in class 4–6 (cf 22). L = 4, F = 10, f = 12, h = 2.

Median = 4 + [(15 − 10) ÷ 12] × 2 = 4 + 0.833 = **4.83 min**.

The median is not affected by extreme values and suits skewed data (for example survival times, income) and ordinal data. It can also be read from an ogive (cumulative frequency curve).

### 1.4.3 Mode

The mode is the value that occurs most often.

Grouped data: Mode = L + [(f1 − f0) ÷ (2f1 − f0 − f2)] × h

where L = lower limit of the modal class (highest frequency), f1 = its frequency, f0 = frequency of the class before, f2 = frequency of the class after.

**Worked example (grouped).** Modal class 4–6: L = 4, f1 = 12, f0 = 7, f2 = 6, h = 2.

Mode = 4 + [(12 − 7) ÷ (24 − 7 − 6)] × 2 = 4 + (5 ÷ 11) × 2 = **4.91 min**.

**Empirical relation** (moderately skewed data): Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean = 3(4.833) − 2(4.8) = 4.90 min, which agrees closely.

A distribution may be unimodal, bimodal (two peaks, for example fast and slow acetylators) or multimodal. The mode is the only average that suits nominal data (most commonly prescribed brand).

### 1.4.4 Other means (brief)

- **Geometric mean (GM)** = nth root of the product of n values; used for ratios, growth rates, titres and log-normally distributed data such as AUC and Cmax in bioequivalence. Example: GM of 2 and 8 = √16 = 4.
- **Harmonic mean (HM)** = n ÷ Σ(1/x); used for averaging rates. Example: HM of 2 and 8 = 2 ÷ (0.5 + 0.125) = 3.2.
- For positive values: AM ≥ GM ≥ HM.

**Choosing the average**

| Situation | Best measure |
| --- | --- |
| Symmetrical numerical data | Mean |
| Skewed data or extreme values present | Median |
| Most common category or size | Mode |
| Ratios, log-normal data | Geometric mean |

## 1.5 Measures of dispersion

**Dispersion** is the extent to which values are scattered around the average. Two batches can have the same mean weight but very different spread; the one with less spread is more uniform. Absolute measures carry the unit of the data; relative measures are unit-free and allow comparison between different data sets.

### 1.5.1 Range

Range = largest value − smallest value. Coefficient of range = (L − S) ÷ (L + S).

Tablet example: range = 255 − 247 = **8 mg**. Simple and quick (used in control charts) but it depends only on two extreme values.

### 1.5.2 Quartile deviation and mean deviation

- Quartile deviation (semi-interquartile range) = (Q3 − Q1) ÷ 2; not affected by extreme values.
- Mean deviation = Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n. Tablet example: Σ|x − 250.5| = 18, so MD = **1.8 mg**.

### 1.5.3 Variance and standard deviation

**Standard deviation (SD)** is the square root of the mean of squared deviations from the mean. It is the most widely used measure of spread.

- Population SD: σ = √[Σ(x − µ)² ÷ N]
- Sample SD: s = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)], using n − 1 (degrees of freedom) because the sample mean has already been estimated from the same data.
- Variance = SD².
- Computing form: Σ(x − x̄)² = Σx² − (Σx)²/n.
- Grouped data: s = √[Σf(x − x̄)² ÷ (N − 1)].

**Worked example (tablets, example numbers).** Mean = 250.5.

| x | 248 | 252 | 250 | 249 | 251 | 250 | 253 | 247 | 250 | 255 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| x − x̄ | −2.5 | 1.5 | −0.5 | −1.5 | 0.5 | −0.5 | 2.5 | −3.5 | −0.5 | 4.5 |
| (x − x̄)² | 6.25 | 2.25 | 0.25 | 2.25 | 0.25 | 0.25 | 6.25 | 12.25 | 0.25 | 20.25 |

Σ(x − x̄)² = 50.5; variance s² = 50.5 ÷ 9 = 5.61; **s = 2.37 mg**.

**Coefficient of variation (CV) or relative standard deviation (RSD)** = (SD ÷ mean) × 100 = (2.37 ÷ 250.5) × 100 = **0.95%**. CV compares spread between data sets with different units or means; analytical precision is reported as % RSD.

**Grouped SD (from the disintegration table).** Σf(x − 4.8)² = 130.8, so s = √(130.8 ÷ 29) = **2.12 min**.

Properties of SD: always positive or zero; unchanged when a constant is added to every value; multiplied by k when every value is multiplied by k; for a normal distribution about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within ±1, ±2 and ±3 SD of the mean.

**Standard error of mean (SEM)** = SD ÷ √n. It measures the precision of the mean, not the spread of the data (detail in Unit 2).

### 1.5.4 Skewness and kurtosis (brief)

- **Skewness** describes lack of symmetry. Positive (right) skew: long tail to the right, mean > median > mode. Negative skew: mean < median < mode. Karl Pearson's coefficient = (mean − mode) ÷ SD.
- **Kurtosis** describes peakedness: leptokurtic (sharp peak), mesokurtic (normal), platykurtic (flat).

## 1.6 Correlation

**Correlation** measures the degree and direction of a linear relationship between two variables. It does not prove cause and effect.

**Types**

| Type | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | Both rise together | Concentration and absorbance |
| Negative | One rises as the other falls | Drug content and storage time |
| Zero | No linear relationship | Tablet colour and hardness |
| Simple / multiple / partial | Two variables / one with several / two with others held constant | |
| Linear / non-linear | Constant / changing ratio of change | |

**Scatter diagram.** Plot pairs (x, y). A narrow upward band shows strong positive correlation; a round cloud shows none.

```text
 strong +ve         strong -ve          no correlation
 y |       .        y | .               y |  .   .  .
   |     .            |   .               | .  .   .
   |   .              |     .             |   .  .   .
   | .                |       .           | .   .  .
   +---------- x      +---------- x       +---------- x
```

### 1.6.1 Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation (r)

r = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ √[Σ(x − x̄)² × Σ(y − ȳ)²]

Computing form: r = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy] ÷ √{[nΣx² − (Σx)²][nΣy² − (Σy)²]}

r lies between −1 and +1. r = +1: perfect positive; r = −1: perfect negative; r = 0: no linear relation. Rough guide: |r| above 0.7 strong, 0.4–0.7 moderate, below 0.4 weak. r² (coefficient of determination) gives the fraction of variation in y explained by x.

**Worked example (example numbers): calibration of a drug by UV**

| Conc x (µg/ml) | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Absorbance y | 0.11 | 0.20 | 0.31 | 0.40 | 0.52 |

n = 5; Σx = 30; Σy = 1.54; Σxy = 11.28; Σx² = 220; Σy² = 0.5786.

- Sxy = Σxy − ΣxΣy/n = 11.28 − (30 × 1.54)/5 = 11.28 − 9.24 = 2.04
- Sxx = Σx² − (Σx)²/n = 220 − 180 = 40
- Syy = Σy² − (Σy)²/n = 0.5786 − 0.47432 = 0.10428

r = 2.04 ÷ √(40 × 0.10428) = 2.04 ÷ 2.0424 = **0.9988**; r² = 0.998. Almost perfect positive linear relation, as expected for Beer–Lambert behaviour.

Properties of r: independent of change of origin and scale; symmetrical (r of x with y = r of y with x); r is the geometric mean of the two regression coefficients (Unit 2).

### 1.6.2 Spearman's rank correlation (ρ)

Used for ranked (ordinal) data or when the data are not normal.

ρ = 1 − [6Σd² ÷ n(n² − 1)], where d = difference between the two ranks of each item.

**Worked example (example numbers).** Two panellists rank six flavoured syrups for taste.

| Syrup | A | B | C | D | E | F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rank by panellist 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| Rank by panellist 2 | 2 | 1 | 4 | 3 | 6 | 5 |
| d² | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

Σd² = 6; ρ = 1 − (6 × 6) ÷ (6 × 35) = 1 − 0.171 = **0.83**, good agreement between panellists. For tied ranks, give each tied value the average of the ranks it would occupy.

**Pharmaceutical uses of correlation:** linearity of analytical methods, in vitro–in vivo correlation (IVIVC: dissolution versus absorption), relation between hardness and disintegration time, dose and response, lipophilicity and absorption.

## 1.7 Remember

- Biostatistics = statistics applied to biology, medicine and pharmacy; descriptive vs inferential.
- Mean = Σx/n; grouped median = L + [(N/2 − F)/f]h; grouped mode = L + [(f1 − f0)/(2f1 − f0 − f2)]h; Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.
- Sample SD uses n − 1; CV (% RSD) = SD/mean × 100; SEM = SD/√n.
- About 68%, 95%, 99.7% of normal data lie within ±1, ±2, ±3 SD.
- r runs from −1 to +1; r² = fraction of variation explained; correlation is not causation.
- Spearman ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/n(n² − 1) for ranks.

# Unit 2: Regression, probability, sampling and parametric tests

This is the heaviest unit of the subject. It moves from describing data to predicting and testing: regression gives an equation to predict one variable from another, probability and its distributions explain how chance behaves, sampling explains how a small group can stand for a whole batch or population, and parametric tests (t-tests and ANOVA) decide whether observed differences are real. Most 10-mark numericals come from here.

All numbers in the worked examples are **example numbers** made up for practice.

## 2.1 Regression

**Regression** is the estimation of the value of one variable (dependent, y) from a known value of another (independent, x) using a mathematical relationship. Correlation tells how strongly two variables are related; regression gives the actual equation for prediction.

| Point | Correlation | Regression |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Degree and direction of relationship | Prediction of one variable from another |
| Variables | Both treated alike | One dependent, one independent |
| Coefficient | r, from −1 to +1, no unit | b (slope), carries units, any value |
| Symmetry | r(xy) = r(yx) | b(yx) ≠ b(xy) |

### 2.1.1 Curve fitting by the method of least squares

The best-fitting line is the one that makes the **sum of squared vertical deviations** (residuals) of observed points from the line the smallest. This is the principle of least squares.

For the line **y = a + bx**, minimising Σ(y − a − bx)² gives two normal equations:

- Σy = na + bΣx
- Σxy = aΣx + bΣx²

Solving them:

- b(yx) = Sxy ÷ Sxx = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy] ÷ [nΣx² − (Σx)²]
- a = ȳ − b x̄ (the line always passes through the point of means x̄, ȳ)

For the line **x = a′ + b′y** (regression of x on y), used to predict x from y:

- b(xy) = Sxy ÷ Syy, and a′ = x̄ − b′ȳ.

Link with correlation: r = ±√[b(yx) × b(xy)], and r takes the sign of the regression coefficients. Both coefficients have the same sign; if one is above 1, the other must be below 1. The two regression lines cross at (x̄, ȳ); they coincide when r = ±1 and are perpendicular when r = 0.

**Worked example (example numbers): UV calibration line**

Data from Unit 1: x = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 µg/ml; y = 0.11, 0.20, 0.31, 0.40, 0.52. Sxy = 2.04, Sxx = 40, Syy = 0.10428, x̄ = 6, ȳ = 0.308.

- b(yx) = 2.04 ÷ 40 = **0.051**; a = 0.308 − 0.051 × 6 = **0.002**
- Regression of y on x: **y = 0.002 + 0.051x**
- Predict: a sample shows absorbance 0.35 → x = (0.35 − 0.002) ÷ 0.051 = **6.82 µg/ml**
- b(xy) = 2.04 ÷ 0.10428 = 19.56; a′ = 6 − 19.56 × 0.308 = −0.025; regression of x on y: **x = −0.025 + 19.56y**
- Check: b(yx) × b(xy) = 0.051 × 19.56 = 0.9977 = r², so r = 0.9988 (same as Unit 1).

### 2.1.2 Standard error of regression (standard error of estimate)

The standard error of estimate measures how far the observed points lie from the regression line on average:

S(y.x) = √[Σ(y − ŷ)² ÷ (n − 2)], with n − 2 degrees of freedom because two constants (a and b) were estimated.

Calibration example: predicted ŷ = 0.104, 0.206, 0.308, 0.410, 0.512; residuals 0.006, −0.006, 0.002, −0.010, 0.008; Σ(residual)² = 0.00024.

S(y.x) = √(0.00024 ÷ 3) = **0.0089** absorbance units. A small value means points lie close to the line. Standard error of the slope = S(y.x) ÷ √Sxx = 0.0089 ÷ √40 = 0.0014 (used for testing the slope in Unit 4).

### 2.1.3 Multiple regression

When y depends on two or more independent variables:

y = b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + … + bkxk

Each partial regression coefficient (b1, b2…) is the change in y for a one-unit change in that x while the other x's are held constant. Coefficients are found by least squares, solving one normal equation per constant. For two variables:

- Σy = nb0 + b1Σx1 + b2Σx2
- Σx1y = b0Σx1 + b1Σx1² + b2Σx1x2
- Σx2y = b0Σx2 + b1Σx1x2 + b2Σx2²

**Worked example (example numbers): tablet hardness y (kg) against compression force x1 (kN) and binder level x2 (%)**

| Run | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| x1 | 5 | 10 | 5 | 10 | 7.5 | 7.5 |
| x2 | 1 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| y | 4.0 | 6.1 | 5.2 | 7.9 | 5.9 | 6.1 |

Sums: n = 6, Σx1 = 45, Σx2 = 12, Σy = 35.2, Σx1² = 362.5, Σx2² = 28, Σx1x2 = 90, Σx1y = 276.0, Σx2y = 73.4.

Solving the three normal equations gives **y = 0.767 + 0.48x1 + 0.75x2**. Hardness rises 0.48 kg for each extra kN of force and 0.75 kg for each extra 1% of binder.

Multiple coefficient of determination R² = 1 − SSE/SST = 1 − 0.163/8.173 = **0.98**: 98% of the variation in hardness is explained by the two variables. Standard error of regression = √[SSE ÷ (n − k − 1)] = √(0.163 ÷ 3) = 0.23 kg.

Pharmaceutical uses of regression: calibration curves and assay, stability (log concentration against time for first-order decay, giving k and shelf life), dose–response and probit analysis, IVIVC, QSAR, predicting formulation responses in design of experiments.

## 2.2 Probability

**Probability** is a number from 0 to 1 that measures how likely an event is. 0 means impossible, 1 means certain.

**Classical (a priori) definition:** P(A) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes.

**Relative frequency (empirical) definition:** P(A) = the limit of (number of times A occurred ÷ number of trials) as trials increase. Example: if 3 of 1000 patients show a rash, P(rash) ≈ 0.003.

**Key terms and rules**

| Term / rule | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Experiment, outcome, sample space | A trial, one result, the set of all results |
| Mutually exclusive events | Cannot occur together (a tablet passes or fails) |
| Independent events | One does not change the chance of the other |
| Addition rule | P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); for exclusive events P(A) + P(B) |
| Multiplication rule | P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events |
| Complement | P(not A) = 1 − P(A) |
| Conditional probability | P(A given B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) |

A **probability distribution** lists every possible value of a random variable with its probability. Discrete examples: binomial and Poisson; continuous example: normal.

### 2.2.1 Binomial distribution

Used when there are n independent trials, each with only two outcomes (success or failure), and the probability of success p stays the same in each trial (q = 1 − p).

P(x successes) = nCx × p^x × q^(n − x)

Mean = np; variance = npq; SD = √npq.

**Worked example (example numbers).** 10% of capsules from a machine are defective. In a sample of 5, find the probabilities.

| Defectives x | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P(x) | 0.5905 | 0.3281 | 0.0729 | 0.0081 | 0.00045 | 0.00001 |

P(no defective) = 0.9^5 = 0.5905; P(at least one) = 1 − 0.5905 = **0.4095**. Mean = 5 × 0.1 = 0.5 defective; variance = 5 × 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.45.

Uses: number of patients responding out of n treated, number of defective units in a sample, acceptance sampling plans.

### 2.2.2 Poisson distribution (brief)

For counts of rare events in a fixed interval when n is large and p small: P(x) = e^(−m) m^x ÷ x!, with mean = variance = m (= np). Examples: particles per ml of an injection, rare adverse reactions, bacterial colonies per plate.

### 2.2.3 Normal distribution

The most important continuous distribution. Many biological measurements (body weight, tablet weight, assay values, errors of measurement) follow it approximately.

Equation: f(x) = [1 ÷ (σ√2π)] × e^[−(x − µ)² / 2σ²]

**Properties**

1. Bell-shaped and symmetrical about the mean.
2. Mean = median = mode, at the centre.
3. Described fully by two parameters, µ and σ.
4. The tails approach the x-axis but never touch it (asymptotic).
5. Total area under the curve = 1.
6. Area within µ ± 1σ = 68.27%, µ ± 1.96σ = 95%, µ ± 2σ = 95.45%, µ ± 2.58σ = 99%, µ ± 3σ = 99.73%.
7. Skewness zero; mesokurtic.
8. Points of inflexion at µ ± σ.

```text
                    _.-'''-._
                 .-'    |    '-.
               .'       |       '.
            _.'         |         '._
      __..-'  |    |    |    |    |  '-..__
   ---+-------+----+----+----+----+-------+---
     -3σ     -2σ  -1σ   µ   +1σ  +2σ     +3σ
              |<--- 68.27% --->|
         |<-------- 95.45% -------->|
```

**Standard normal variable:** z = (x − µ) ÷ σ, which has mean 0 and SD 1. Areas are read from z tables.

**Worked example (example numbers).** Tablet weights are normal with mean 250 mg and SD 5 mg.

- P(240 to 260 mg): z = ±2, area = **0.9545** (95.45% of tablets).
- P(more than 258 mg): z = (258 − 250) ÷ 5 = 1.6; area beyond z = 1.6 is **0.0548**, so about 5.5% of tablets.
- P(245 to 255 mg): z = ±1, area = 0.6827.

The normal distribution is the basis of z-tests, confidence intervals, control charts and most parametric tests; by the **central limit theorem**, means of large samples are close to normal even if the original data are not.

## 2.3 Sampling

### 2.3.1 Terms

- **Population (universe):** all units of interest. Finite (all tablets in batch B-101) or infinite.
- **Sample:** the part actually examined.
- **Large sample:** usually n ≥ 30; tested with the z (normal) test.
- **Small sample:** n < 30; tested with t, F and chi-square tests, which allow for extra uncertainty.
- **Sampling frame:** the list from which the sample is drawn.

**Essence (need) of sampling.** Studying every unit is often impossible or pointless: tests may destroy the product (assay, dissolution), populations may be huge, and time and money are limited. A well-drawn sample gives reliable results faster and cheaper, and with care (fewer units) the measurements can be more accurate. Good sampling needs a representative sample, an adequate size, independence of units and no bias.

### 2.3.2 Types of sampling

| Type | How it works | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Probability sampling** | Every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection | |
| Simple random | Lottery or random-number table; every unit has an equal chance | Picking 20 tablets from a batch by random numbers |
| Systematic | Every kth unit after a random start | Every 100th tablet off the press |
| Stratified | Population split into similar groups (strata); random sample from each | Sampling from beginning, middle and end of a batch |
| Cluster | Groups (clusters) chosen at random, all units in them studied | Choosing whole villages in a survey |
| Multistage | Random selection in stages | District → village → household |
| **Non-probability sampling** | Selection chance not known; risk of bias | |
| Convenience | Units easiest to reach | Patients attending one clinic |
| Purposive (judgement) | Chosen by the investigator's judgement | Experts for a panel |
| Quota | Fixed numbers from each category, chosen non-randomly | 50 men, 50 women |
| Snowball | Subjects recruit others | Rare-disease patients |

**Sampling error** is the difference between a sample statistic and the population parameter due to chance; it falls as sample size rises. **Non-sampling errors** come from bias, faulty measurement, non-response or recording mistakes.

### 2.3.3 Standard error of mean (SEM)

SEM = σ ÷ √n (estimated by s ÷ √n). It is the SD of the distribution of sample means. A small SEM means the sample mean is a precise estimate of µ. SEM is used to build confidence intervals and in t and z tests.

**Example.** Ten tablets: s = 2.37 mg. SEM = 2.37 ÷ √10 = **0.75 mg**.

95% confidence interval for µ (large sample): x̄ ± 1.96 SEM; for a small sample: x̄ ± t(0.05, n − 1) × SEM.

SD vs SEM: SD describes the spread of individual values; SEM describes the precision of the mean. Report "mean ± SD" to describe data and "mean ± SEM" or a confidence interval when comparing means.

## 2.4 Testing of hypothesis

**Hypothesis:** a statement about a population parameter that can be tested with sample data.

- **Null hypothesis (H0):** there is no difference or no effect (new and old formulations dissolve equally; µ1 = µ2).
- **Alternative hypothesis (H1 or Ha):** there is a difference (µ1 ≠ µ2, two-tailed) or a difference in one stated direction (µ1 > µ2, one-tailed).

**Level of significance (α):** the risk we accept of rejecting a true H0, commonly 0.05 (5%) or 0.01 (1%). **P value:** the probability of getting a result at least this extreme if H0 were true. Reject H0 when P < α.

**Errors in testing**

| Decision | H0 true | H0 false |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reject H0 | **Type I error (α)**: false positive | Correct (power = 1 − β) |
| Accept H0 | Correct (1 − α) | **Type II error (β)**: false negative |

- Type I error: concluding a drug works when it does not, or rejecting a good batch. In quality control α is called the producer's risk.
- Type II error: missing a real effect (concluding a useful drug does not work), or accepting a bad batch. In quality control β is called the consumer's risk.
- **Power** = 1 − β, the chance of detecting a real difference; usually set at 80% or 90%. Increasing sample size lowers both risks together.

**Steps of a test of significance**

1. State H0 and H1.
2. Choose α (0.05) and decide one- or two-tailed.
3. Choose the test (z, t, F, chi-square, non-parametric) and compute the test statistic.
4. Find the critical (table) value for the degrees of freedom.
5. If |calculated| ≥ critical (or P < α), reject H0; otherwise do not reject it.
6. State the conclusion in words.

**Degrees of freedom (df):** the number of values free to vary after constraints are fixed; for one sample, df = n − 1.

**Large-sample z-test for a mean:** z = (x̄ − µ) ÷ (σ/√n). Example (example numbers): 100 tablets give mean 248.6 mg, SD 6 mg; label claim 250 mg. z = (248.6 − 250) ÷ (6/10) = −2.33. |z| > 1.96, so the mean differs significantly from 250 mg at the 5% level.

## 2.5 Parametric tests

**Parametric tests** assume that data are quantitative, come from a normally distributed population, the samples are random and independent, and (for comparing groups) the variances are equal (homogeneity of variance). They use the mean and SD and are more powerful than non-parametric tests when these assumptions hold.

### 2.5.1 Student's t-test

Developed by W.S. Gosset ("Student") for small samples. The t distribution is symmetrical and bell-shaped like the normal but has heavier tails; it approaches the normal as df increases.

**(a) One-sample t-test** — compares a sample mean with a known or claimed value.

t = (x̄ − µ) ÷ (s/√n), df = n − 1

**Worked example (example numbers).** Assay of six tablets (% of label claim): 98.2, 99.1, 97.5, 98.8, 99.4, 97.9. Does the mean differ from 100%?

- x̄ = 98.48; Σ(x − x̄)² = 2.708; s = √(2.708/5) = 0.736; SEM = 0.736/√6 = 0.300
- t = (98.48 − 100) ÷ 0.300 = **−5.05**, df = 5
- Table t(0.05, 5) = 2.571. |t| > 2.571, so reject H0: the mean assay is significantly below 100% (P ≈ 0.004).

**(b) Unpaired (independent, pooled) t-test** — compares means of two independent groups.

Pooled variance: sp² = [Σ(x1 − x̄1)² + Σ(x2 − x̄2)²] ÷ (n1 + n2 − 2)

t = (x̄1 − x̄2) ÷ √[sp²(1/n1 + 1/n2)], df = n1 + n2 − 2

**Worked example (example numbers).** Percent drug dissolved at 30 min:

| Formulation A | 82 | 85 | 79 | 88 | 84 | 86 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Formulation B | 76 | 80 | 74 | 79 | 77 | 82 |

- A: mean 84.0, Σ(x − x̄)² = 50.0; B: mean 78.0, Σ(x − x̄)² = 42.0
- sp² = (50 + 42) ÷ 10 = 9.2; sp = 3.03
- SE of difference = √[9.2(1/6 + 1/6)] = 1.751
- t = (84 − 78) ÷ 1.751 = **3.43**, df = 10; table t(0.05, 10) = 2.228
- Reject H0: A dissolves significantly faster than B (P ≈ 0.006).
- Check equal variances with the F ratio: 10.0/8.4 = 1.19, below F(5,5) = 5.05, so pooling is fair.

**(c) Paired t-test** — compares two related measurements on the same subjects (before and after, crossover).

d = difference for each pair; t = d̄ ÷ (sd/√n), df = n − 1 (n = number of pairs)

**Worked example (example numbers).** Diastolic BP (mm Hg) of six patients before and after a drug:

| Patient | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before | 96 | 100 | 92 | 104 | 98 | 95 |
| After | 90 | 94 | 90 | 96 | 93 | 92 |
| d | 6 | 6 | 2 | 8 | 5 | 3 |

- d̄ = 30/6 = 5.0; Σ(d − d̄)² = 24; sd = √(24/5) = 2.19; SE = 2.19/√6 = 0.894
- t = 5.0 ÷ 0.894 = **5.59**, df = 5; table value 2.571
- Reject H0: the drug lowers diastolic BP significantly (P ≈ 0.003).

Pairing removes the variation between patients, which is why a paired design is more sensitive than comparing two separate groups.

### 2.5.2 F-test for two variances

F = larger variance ÷ smaller variance, with df (n1 − 1, n2 − 1). Used to check equality of variances (precision of two methods or two analysts) and as the basis of ANOVA.

### 2.5.3 Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

Repeating t-tests for three or more groups raises the overall chance of a Type I error. **ANOVA**, developed by R.A. Fisher, compares several means in one test by splitting the total variation into parts due to known sources and a part due to chance (error).

**Assumptions:** normal populations, equal variances, independent random samples, additive effects.

#### One-way ANOVA (one factor)

| Source | SS | df | MS = SS/df | F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Between groups (treatments) | SSB | k − 1 | MSB | MSB/MSW |
| Within groups (error) | SSW | N − k | MSW | |
| Total | SST | N − 1 | | |

Computing steps: G = grand total; correction factor CF = G²/N; SST = Σx² − CF; SSB = Σ(Ti²/ni) − CF, where Ti = group total; SSW = SST − SSB.

**Worked example (example numbers).** Tablet hardness (kg) with three binders, four tablets each:

| Binder | Values | Total | Mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PVP | 5.1, 5.4, 5.0, 5.3 | 20.8 | 5.2 |
| Starch | 6.2, 6.0, 6.5, 6.1 | 24.8 | 6.2 |
| MCC | 5.6, 5.9, 5.5, 5.8 | 22.8 | 5.7 |

- G = 68.4; N = 12; CF = 68.4²/12 = 389.88; Σx² = 392.22
- SST = 392.22 − 389.88 = 2.34
- SSB = (20.8² + 24.8² + 22.8²)/4 − 389.88 = 391.88 − 389.88 = 2.00
- SSW = 2.34 − 2.00 = 0.34

| Source | SS | df | MS | F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Between binders | 2.00 | 2 | 1.000 | **26.5** |
| Within (error) | 0.34 | 9 | 0.0378 | |
| Total | 2.34 | 11 | | |

Table F(2, 9) at 5% = 4.26. F calculated is far greater, so the binders give significantly different hardness.

#### Least significant difference (LSD)

ANOVA says "the means differ" but not which ones. The LSD (Fisher's) test compares pairs after a significant F:

LSD = t(α, error df) × √(2 × MSE ÷ n)

Example: LSD = 2.262 × √(2 × 0.0378 ÷ 4) = 2.262 × 0.1374 = **0.31 kg**.

Differences between means: Starch − PVP = 1.0; Starch − MCC = 0.5; MCC − PVP = 0.5. All exceed 0.31, so every pair differs; starch gives the hardest tablets. (Other post-hoc tests: Tukey, Duncan, Bonferroni, Dunnett for comparison with one control.)

#### Two-way ANOVA (two factors)

Two sources of variation are studied together, for example formulation (rows) and analyst or day (columns, often a block). Without replication:

| Source | SS | df | F |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rows (factor A) | SSR | r − 1 | MSR/MSE |
| Columns (factor B) | SSC | c − 1 | MSC/MSE |
| Error (residual) | SSE | (r − 1)(c − 1) | |
| Total | SST | rc − 1 | |

SSR = Σ(row total²)/c − CF; SSC = Σ(column total²)/r − CF; SSE = SST − SSR − SSC.

**Worked example (example numbers).** Assay (%) of three formulations, each tested by four analysts:

| Formulation | Analyst 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | Row total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F1 | 98.5 | 99.4 | 98.2 | 99.0 | 395.1 |
| F2 | 100.2 | 100.3 | 99.6 | 100.9 | 401.0 |
| F3 | 99.1 | 99.9 | 98.7 | 99.4 | 397.1 |
| Column total | 297.8 | 299.6 | 296.5 | 299.3 | G = 1193.2 |

CF = 1193.2²/12 = 118643.853; Σx² = 118650.820.

| Source | SS | df | MS | F | F table (5%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Formulations | 4.502 | 2 | 2.251 | **33.3** | 5.14 |
| Analysts | 2.060 | 3 | 0.687 | **10.2** | 4.76 |
| Error | 0.405 | 6 | 0.0675 | | |
| Total | 6.967 | 11 | | | |

Both formulations and analysts differ significantly. Taking analysts out as a separate source made the error smaller, so the formulation comparison became more sensitive. With replication, two-way ANOVA also tests the **interaction** (A × B): whether the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other.

## 2.6 Remember

- Least squares: y = a + bx, b = Sxy/Sxx, a = ȳ − bx̄; r² = b(yx) × b(xy).
- Standard error of estimate = √[Σ(y − ŷ)²/(n − 2)].
- Binomial: nCx p^x q^(n−x), mean np, variance npq. Normal: z = (x − µ)/σ; 68–95–99.7 rule.
- Large sample ≥ 30 → z test; small sample → t test.
- Type I = reject true H0 (α); Type II = accept false H0 (β); power = 1 − β.
- One-sample t = (x̄ − µ)/(s/√n); unpaired uses pooled variance, df n1 + n2 − 2; paired uses differences, df n − 1.
- ANOVA: CF = G²/N; F = MS(between)/MS(error); LSD = t × √(2MSE/n) after a significant F.
